title: Iteration
examples: How do I know if it will actually converge?
What is the difference between iterating and solving?
Can I use this method for any function?

explain.say: Today we look at a method called iteration for finding roots. We start by rearranging an equation into the form x equals g of x. For example, if we want to solve x squared equals 25, we can write it as x equals the square root of 25. But that is not helpful for iteration.

A better way to rearrange is to isolate x on one side. If we have x squared equals 25, we can rewrite it as x equals 25 divided by x. This gives us our function g of x. So, g of x equals 25 divided by x.

Iteration means repeatedly applying the function g of x. We start with a guess, say x one. Then we calculate x two using g of x one. Then x three uses g of x two. This sequence is x one, x two, x three, and so on.

Convergence means that as we repeat the process, the values get closer and closer to a single specific number. If it converges, that number is a root of the original equation. For example, if the root is 5, the sequence will approach 5.

Imagine you are trying to find the average weight of a group of students. You guess a number, then use the formula to get a better guess. Repeating this process gets you very close to the true average weight.

faq.q: What is the starting value x one?
faq.a: The starting value x one is just an initial guess. You should pick a number that you think is close to the actual root. Another way to ask this is what is the initial guess? You could also ask what do I use for x one?
asks: What do I use for x one?

faq.q: Does it always converge to the right answer?
faq.a: Not always. The convergence depends on how you rearranged the equation. Sometimes, if you pick a poor starting value, the sequence might move away from the root. You might ask if it always works, or what if it doesn't converge?

faq.q: How do I know if the process has stopped?
faq.a: You stop when the values become very close to each other. You can check if the difference between two consecutive terms is smaller than a tiny number. You might ask when is it accurate enough, or how accurate should I be?

faq.q: Can I use this if the function is complicated?
faq.a: Yes, you can use it for many functions. The key is successfully rearranging the equation into the form x equals g of x. You might ask what functions can I use, or is there a limit to this method?
asks: Is there a limit to this method?

faq.q: Is iteration the same as using a calculator's solve button?
faq.a: No, they are different methods. Iteration is a process of repeating a formula you derive. The calculator button uses more complex built-in algorithms. You might ask what is the difference from a calculator, or is it the same thing?
asks: What is the difference from a calculator?

facts: Iteration requires rearranging the equation to the form x equals g of x.
The process involves repeatedly calculating the next value using the function g of x.
Convergence means the sequence of values approaches a fixed root.
The initial guess x one can affect whether the process converges.

quiz.say: To find the root of x squared equals 16, which function g(x) should you use for iteration?
quiz.why: We rearrange x squared equals 16 to get x equals 16 divided by x, which is g(x).

wrong.0: This is a linear rearrangement, not derived from the original x squared form.
wrong.2: This adds the x term, which is not part of the original equation structure.
wrong.3: This incorrectly applies the square root to the entire fraction.

quiz.say: If you use g(x) equals x plus one over two x, and start at x one equals 1, what is the next value, x two?
quiz.why: Plugging x one equals 1 into g(x) gives 1 plus one divided by two, which equals 1.5.

wrong.0: This only calculates the fraction part and ignores the starting x value.
wrong.2: This incorrectly doubles the starting value.
wrong.3: This forgets to add the initial x value to the fraction.

quiz.say: If the sequence generated by iteration is 2.8, 2.81, 2.812, what does this suggest about the root?
quiz.why: Because the values are getting closer together, the sequence is converging to that value.

wrong.0: The values are clearly getting closer, which shows convergence, not failure.
wrong.2: The values are changing, so the root is not exactly the first number shown.
wrong.3: This guesses a whole number without checking the pattern of the sequence.
